This enormous cheddar cheese block measured four feet wide and two feet tall. It weighed fourteen hundred pounds, which is about as much as a large horse!

Where did this chunk of cheddar come from? In 1835, a dairy farmer named Thomas Meacham made it as a gift for President Andrew Jackson. Before delivering it to the White House, Meacham took the cheese on tour. He showed it off in New York, Philadelphia, and Baltimore. Finally, it arrived at the White House, where it was displayed for over a year.

President Jackson welcomed the gift, but he wasn't sure what to do with it. In 1837, he was getting ready to move out of the White House. So, he decided to share his cheddar treasure. On February 22, Jackson held a huge public party. About ten thousand people showed up to meet the president, talk with government leaders, and, of course, eat cheese. In less than two hours, the cheese block was gone! However, the strong cheesy smell stayed around for much longer. The next president had to remove the curtains, paint the walls, and air out the carpet to get rid of the odor.

The scent of the cheese eventually faded. However, the memory of Jackson's famous party has lived on in other ways. Unlike Jackson's event, Big Block of Cheese Day did not include actual cheese or a White House party. Instead of chatting with people over a plate of cheddar, government leaders connected with people online. They listened to ideas and answered questions that people sent to them on the internet. The event was a success, and Big Block of Cheese Day continued for two more years.

passage.text: From books and billboards to text messages and T-shirts, writing seems to be everywhere. But this wasn't always the case. Before writing could show up on pages and screens, it had to be invented.

Historians believe that writing was first invented before 3000 BCE. It began in a place called Sumer, located in what is now Iraq and Iran. At first, writing was mostly used by traders. These traders needed a way to keep records when they traded goods like sheep or grain. So, the first writings were simple drawings of things like places, animals, or crops. These drawings were often followed by marks to show an amount. An early Sumerian text might have a picture of a temple, a sheep, and three lines. This would remind a trader that he had traded three sheep to someone at the temple.

The early Sumerian writing system was good for representing physical objects that could be seen and touched. However, it had no markings for abstract things like thoughts or emotions. Did these early writers enjoy being traders? We don't know. The Sumerians could keep lists, but they could not yet use writing to describe events or tell stories.

Starting around 3200 BCE, writing began to change. Some ancient peoples began creating symbols to represent the sounds in their spoken language. The symbols worked like an alphabet, though they looked different from the symbols used in today's alphabets. When writers put the symbols together, they were able to build any word in their spoken language. Suddenly it became possible to write about ideas and stories, not just objects and amounts.

passage.text: When you are going through a difficult time, sometimes a piece of candy can help cheer you up. That is especially true if the candy comes falling out of the sky. Sound impossible? Well, for some children living in West Berlin from 1948 to 1949, that is exactly what happened.

After World War II, the capital city of Germany was divided into East and West Berlin. The eastern part of the city was controlled by Russia. The western part was controlled by France, Britain, and the U.S. However, in 1948, Russia tried to force the other countries to leave the city. The Russians blocked all of the usual trade and supply routes into West Berlin. The people of West Berlin feared they would soon run out of food and supplies. Then the U.S. and other countries created Operation Vittles, a plan to fly food and other supplies into the city.

Each day, planes would deliver as many as eight thousand tons of supplies to West Berlin. One of the pilots responsible for this work was an American named Gail Halvorsen. During one delivery, Halvorsen met a group of West Berlin children who had gathered to watch the planes. Before returning to the air, Halvorsen gave the children some sticks of chewing gum. It wasn't much, but the children were very grateful. Suddenly Halvorsen had an idea. He told the children that he would drop them some more candy from his plane the next day.

Halvorsen tied the candy packages to small parachutes made from handkerchiefs. The packages dropped gently from the plane to the children on the ground. Afterward, the children talked excitedly about the wonderful "Chocolate Flyer" who dropped candy from the sky. Halvorsen decided to make candy airdrops a regular event. Soon, other pilots began to join Halvorsen, and Operation Little Vittles was born.

Eventually, news about the pilots' actions began to spread. Many people who heard about the candy airdrops wanted to help sustain them. American candy companies sent the pilots free candy, and school children in America made small cloth parachutes. Thanks to this effort, Operation Little Vittles continued for months, until supply routes finally reopened in 1949. For years afterward, the children of West Berlin continued to send thank you letters to Halvorsen and the other pilots. These pilots had not just given the children candy; they had given them something to look forward to during a difficult and uncertain time.

passage.text: "GOAL!" shouts the announcer. Thousands of fans begin to cheer. The women on the soccer field start to jump, run, and hug one another in victory. Today, scenes like this are common in many countries. However, there was a time when soccer was thought to be a game only for men.

Modern soccer, known as football outside the U.S., became popular in England and Scotland starting in the 1700s. By the 1870s, men's teams were playing in front of large, paying crowds. Women played, too, but not publicly. Things began to change in the late 1800s, when female players started joining together to form teams and leagues.

One of the most famous women's teams was created in 1895. It was called the British Ladies' Football Club (BLFC). The team was started by several talented players with the help of a woman named Lady Florence Dixie. Though Dixie wasn't a soccer player herself, she wanted to make life more equitable for women. She thought that female athletes deserved the same chance to play sports that male athletes had. She wanted women to be able to show their athletic talents to the world, too.

The BLFC got a lot of attention, both positive and negative. Some of the members played under made-up names, such as Nettie Honeyball. When the BLFC played its first game in London, a crowd of ten thousand people came to watch. A few newspaper reporters were excited by the game and wrote that it proved how well women could play. However, other reporters wrote negative things about the BLFC game and the women playing in it. They wrote that soccer was too rough for women. A few even refused to believe that all of the talented players were actually women.

Female soccer players have faced many challenges over the years. Between 1921 and 1971, most places in England refused to let women's teams play on their fields. For over sixty years, women's teams also could not play in the world's biggest soccer competition, the World Cup. However, female players never stopped fighting for the right to play the sport they loved. The Women's World Cup was finally created in 1991, and since then, women's soccer has grown more and more popular. By refusing to give up, female soccer players have changed people's ideas about the things that women can do.
